name: Prize crossword No 25,340
preamble: Asterisked clues lack a definition; their solutions share a final destination found elsewhere in the completed grid.

clue.text: Principle of retributive justice bags large Republican vote?

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it inside a sack, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: karma is the idea that your deeds come back to you
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican
a voter marks a ballot with a cross

explanation.surface: A party's punitive policy is smuggling in a big Republican vote.
explanation.walkthrough: Asterisked: no definition. The answer is one of those buried in the destination answer, Highgate Cemetery; the question mark admits the clue has no definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble supplies the meaning: the philosopher Karl Marx lies in Highgate Cemetery in north London.

clue.text: Number of people admitted to empty carriage on Metropolitan Line includes first to exit after drunk remains there

indicators.note: coming after something means being placed later, so one chunk follows another

the leading letter of the following word is the one taken

a gate is the attendance at a sports match
the outside letters of the word
the word cut to its first three letters, the familiar short form, as in the Met Police
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A rail-themed tale: an empty Metropolitan Line carriage takes on passengers, and something left behind by a drunk stays aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: The Metropolitan Line is a London Underground line, which makes 'Number of people admitted' read as passengers; in fact a gate is a crowd figure at a game. This is the shared destination the asterisked clues need.
explanation.definitionFit: A burial ground is the spot where the bodies of the dead are laid to rest, so it is where human remains stay.

clue.text: Bottle lost in a farce

indicators.note: something lost has gone astray, so these letters wander out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bottle goes missing in the middle of a stage comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost in' reads as a stage prop going missing during a farce, but 'lost' is the shuffle signal and 'in' just joins definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A carafe is a glass vessel for serving wine or water at table, a kind of decanter.

clue.text: A fool put wrong setter above measure

indicators.note: putting something wrong means misplacing it, so these letters need to be rearranged

blocks.note: the eight letters, taken as written
a second route to the same name: Paul is a fellow Guardian setter, and a foot is a measure, placed below it in this down entry

explanation.surface: Someone foolishly ranks a crossword setter over a unit of measure.
explanation.walkthrough: Asterisked, so no definition; instead there are two complete routes to the answer, a rearrangement of the first three words and a fellow setter's pseudonym above a unit of length.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble supplies the meaning: the campaigning journalist Paul Foot is buried in Highgate Cemetery.

explanation.surface: A crossword setter walks into a town well on the way to being drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for tipsy and reads as one word, but it splits into 'half' and 'cut'. Halifax is a town in West Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Halifax is a West Yorkshire market and mill town, home of the building society of that name.

clue.text: See 24
Claptrap backed by some lethal blows

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only part of it, so the letters sit inside the words
something backed goes in the opposite direction, so read the letters right to left

blocks.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Empty talk is followed by deadly punches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed by' looks like a phrase meaning supported by, but 'backed' is the turnaround signal and 'by' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean empty, pretentious nonsense: talk that sounds impressive but has no substance.

clue.text: Awards detailed "excellent toilet", except for one holding company

indicators.note: de-tailed means with the tail removed, so the last letter goes
everything except a single I, the Roman one, so that letter is removed
to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece goes within another

explanation.surface: A review hands out prizes, praising a lavatory in detail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' reads as thorough, but it is de-tailed: remove the tail. 'One' is I, the Roman numeral, taken out of LADIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Accolades are honours or tributes given in recognition of merit, so prizes and awards.

clue.text: First of tall stories about first mate ringing topless joint

indicators.note: without a top means the opening letter is removed
to ring something is to encircle it, so one piece goes round another
only the leading letter of the next word is taken

the wrist is a joint; its top letter goes
the opening letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A yarn-spinner's opening tale about a ship's first mate and a dodgy smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: Asterisked, so no definition. 'China' for mate is Cockney rhyming slang (china plate = mate); 'first' tells you the mate-and-joint half comes before the rearranged stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble supplies the meaning: the Victorian poet Christina Rossetti is buried in Highgate Cemetery.

clue.text: Head of state leaving wine district very sober

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter
something leaving goes away, so that letter is taken out

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
A wine region near Bordeaux

explanation.surface: A president steps away from a vineyard region entirely sober.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of state' sounds like a president, but it means only the first letter of state, which falls off the end of the wine region.
explanation.definitionFit: Grave describes someone solemn and serious in manner, intensely sober rather than merely not drunk.

clue.text: Relish belting out Gilbert & Sullivan leads

indicators.note: the leading letters are the first ones, so each name gives its opening letter

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of each name

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys singing Gilbert and Sullivan's principal parts at full volume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belting out' reads as singing loudly, but 'belting' is the shuffle signal and 'out' is fodder. Gilbert and Sullivan wrote comic operas.
explanation.definitionFit: Relish and gusto both mean hearty enjoyment or zest in doing something.

clue.text: Place for skis when travelling in small jumper and dress, after change of heart

and simply adds one thing to the next

explanation.surface: Packing for a ski trip: a little sweater and a frock, and then second thoughts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small jumper' looks like a child's sweater (jumper is British for sweater), but here it is a shortened kangaroo.
explanation.definitionFit: A rack fixed on top of a car carries bulky luggage such as skis on a journey.

clue.text: Fool with hard material

blocks.note: a clot is a stupid person
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: An idiot clutching some tough fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard material' reads as one phrase, but 'hard' belongs to the wordplay. Clot is mild British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth is woven or knitted fabric, the stuff from which garments are sewn.

clue.text: A female tennis player

blocks.note: taken as written
she is the female pronoun

explanation.surface: A woman who plays tennis.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a female player, but Arthur Ashe, the 1975 Wimbledon champion, was a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe was an American who won three Grand Slam singles titles.

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone begins counterfeiting banknotes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forging notes' reads as faking money, but forging is the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An onset is the beginning of something, as in the onset of winter.

blocks.note: a set-to is a quarrel
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Etc' looks like part of the definition, but it is the fodder placed inside the argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Octettes are ensembles of eight performers, a type of musical group.

clue.text: Whip with a bit of elastic rope

indicators.note: a bit of something is a piece of it, so the letters are part of the words

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Lashing out with a length of bungee cord.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a whip made of rope; the answer runs across the join of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A riding crop is a short whip used by horse riders.

Forge some money? It tops your "previous"

taken as written

explanation.surface: Is a forger's workshop where you make cash? It beats your last effort.
explanation.walkthrough: This parse is uncertain. Thy is the old, previous form of your, hence the quotation marks; the reading of 'some money' as SM is a guess.
explanation.definitionFit: A smithy is a blacksmith's workshop, which contains a forge and is often called one.

clue.text: Vitality low when returning to pub

blocks.note: to low is to moo like a cow
PH is the map abbreviation for public house

explanation.surface: Someone's energy sags on going back to the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks like an adjective about mood, but it is the verb for a cow's call.
explanation.definitionFit: Oomph is informal for energy, zest or liveliness.

clue.text: Young ones in love with bartering system

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Young people in love take part in a swap scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Young ones' sounds like children; it is baby birds. 'With' gives W rather than linking.
explanation.definitionFit: Owlets are baby owls, so they are the young offspring of that bird.

clue.text: Nuptials arranged to accommodate a prolific letter writer

taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter writer' suggests a correspondent; the epistles of the New Testament make the apostle the author.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Paul wrote many of the New Testament epistles, letters to early churches.
